sculpture.name: doll
sculpture.title: doll
sculpture.reason: The image shows a handmade cloth doll dressed in Garifuna-style masquerade attire (mask, ribbons, feathered bandana, shell decoration) attributed by the museum to a Garifuna maker, consistent with known Garifuna dance/mask costume traditions.

garment.name: skirt
garment.title: skirt
garment.reason: A red gingham wrap skirt identified by the museum as a "gudu," a traditional Garifuna women's garment, with the museum's own record stating it was made by the Garifuna. This is a clear ethnic garment match.

garment.name: hat
garment.title: hat
garment.reason: A finely plaited jippy jappa palm-fibre hat with open-work sides and a ribbon tie, museum-attributed as made by Garifuna craftspeople; this matches known Garifuna basketry/hat-making traditions.

garment.name: smock; tunic
garment.title: smock; tunic
garment.reason: A green gingham child's smock/tunic explicitly identified by the museum as Garinagu-made "dashiki," a traditional garment type worn by Garifuna children in Guatemala/Belize; clearly photographed and well fitting the claimed ethnicity and category.

garment.name: dance-head-dress
garment.title: dance-head-dress
garment.reason: A dance headdress made of cardboard covered in cotton fabric, decorated with rolled tissue-paper flowers and feathers, attributed to Garifuna makers — consistent with Garifuna festival/dance costume traditions.

garment.name: dress; gown
garment.title: dress; gown
garment.reason: A simple shift dress ("gown") with white bodice and red gingham skirt, explicitly identified by the museum as made and worn by Garinagu (Garifuna) women; this style is a recognized traditional Garifuna dress.

garment.name: smock; tunic
garment.title: smock; tunic
garment.reason: A mint-green, white-trimmed men's smock identified by the museum as Garinagu-made "dashiki" style garment, matching claimed Garifuna dress and craft.

garment.name: smock; tunic
garment.title: smock; tunic
garment.reason: A green gingham child's smock ("dashiki") explicitly made by Garifuna makers, matching the claimed ethnicity and category.

instruments.name: maraca
instruments.title: maraca
instruments.reason: A gourd maraca with a painted wooden handle, a traditional rattle used in Garifuna music (e.g., punta); museum documentation credits it to Garifuna makers. Matches the claimed people and category.

instruments.name: drum
instruments.title: drum
instruments.reason: A Segundo drum with the traditional hollowed hardwood body, deerskin head, and painted Garifuna flag motif, documented as made by the Garifuna — a characteristic instrument of their culture.

instruments.name: maraca
instruments.title: maraca
instruments.reason: A gourd maraca with carved wooden handle, a traditional instrument documented as made by the Garifuna; this matches the claimed ethnicity.

instruments.name: maraca
instruments.title: maraca
instruments.reason: A gourd maraca (sisira) with wooden handle, painted with a Garifuna drummer scene and the Garifuna flag, explicitly identified by the museum as Garifuna-made; this is a genuine Garifuna instrument.

instruments.name: drum
instruments.title: drum
instruments.reason: A handmade single-headed wooden drum with deerskin head and rope tensioning, a type traditionally made and played by the Garifuna; museum credits maker as Garifuna.

instruments.name: maraca
instruments.title: maraca
instruments.reason: A gourd maraca (sisira) with wooden handle, painted with a toucan and "Warasa, Belize" text, explicitly identified as Garifuna-made; a classic Garifuna musical instrument used in ritual and social music.

instruments.name: drum
instruments.title: drum
instruments.reason: The image shows a wooden cylindrical drum with a deerskin head laced with rope, consistent with the Garifuna wooden drums (primero/segunda) used in traditional music; the museum records it as made by the Garifuna.

household.name: sifter
household.title: sifter
household.reason: A round plaited palm-fibre sifter with a wood-and-fibre-wrapped rim, a traditional Garifuna basketry item used in cassava processing, matching the museum's attribution.

household.name: basket
household.title: basket
household.reason: A round wicker basket made of palm fiber ("tie-tie") using traditional wicker-work technique, explicitly attributed by the museum to Garifuna makers — a craft consistent with Garifuna basketry traditions.

household.name: bowl
household.title: bowl
household.reason: This is a painted calabash (gourd) drinking bowl depicting a traditional thatched Garifuna building with drums under the eaves, inscribed "Warasa, Belize" — a documented Garifuna craft object and daily-use vessel type, not clay despite the record's "ceramic" label.

household.name: grater
household.title: grater
household.reason: Close-up of a wooden cassava grater surface inlaid with embedded stone chips, a well-documented traditional Garifuna household tool used for processing cassava (yuca), matching both the claimed ethnicity and the museum's attribution.

masks-ritual.name: dance-mask
masks-ritual.title: dance-mask
masks-ritual.reason: A wire-mesh dance mask with painted face, used for masked dance performance and attributed by the museum's production records to the Garifuna; this fits Garifuna Yancunú (John Canoe) dance mask traditions.

masks-ritual.name: dance-mask
masks-ritual.title: dance-mask
masks-ritual.reason: A wire-mesh dance mask with painted facial features, explicitly attributed by the museum to Garifuna production and consistent with known Garifuna wire-mesh masquerade masks used in Wanaragua/Jankunú dance traditions.
